title: The Great Dosa Debate: Fork and Knife, Center or Side, and Why It All Matters
excerpt: A series of viral videos — from a retired officer cutting dosa with cutlery to a comedian's tactical breakdown of center vs. side eating — has reignited one of Indian food culture's most passionate arguments.
body:
• A series of viral videos have reignited one of Indian food culture's most passionate debates: is there a right way to eat a dosa?
  • A retired military officer's video eating masala dosa with a fork and knife drew 4.3 million views and widespread outrage — while comedian Saikiran's "center vs. side" eating debate divided dosa lovers along strategic lines
  • The broader conversation reflects a tension between Western dining etiquette and traditional Indian hand-eating customs that plays out across the diaspora
  • Food experts say the dosa was designed to be eaten with hands, and the ritual of tearing, dunking, and assembling each bite is part of what makes the dish what it is

Few foods carry as much cultural weight per square inch as the dosa. And few topics unite Indians in passionate disagreement quite like the question of how to eat one properly.

A string of viral videos over the past year has turned dosa-eating etiquette into one of social media's most spirited food debates, touching on everything from thermal engineering to colonial dining norms to the deeply personal question of whether you are a center eater or a side eater.

The Fork and Knife Incident

The debate's most explosive moment came when a retired Indian military officer posted a video of himself eating masala dosa with a fork and knife. Shared on Instagram by the handle @shadowsofchinar, the clip — captioned "Masala Dosa being murdered by fork and knife" — racked up 4.3 million views and thousands of comments that ranged from horrified to genuinely entertained.

"Bro, I am not even South Indian, but I am offended on their behalf," wrote one commenter. "Even the chutney must be crying," added another. The officer, unfazed, called it an "old fauji habit."

"No Hindi, no Tamil. Everyone will unite here to protest."

— Instagram commenter on the viral fork-and-knife dosa video

The video struck a nerve because it inverted a norm that most Indians consider non-negotiable: dosa is hand food. The crisp exterior is meant to be torn, not sliced. The chutney is for dunking, not dabbing. The entire experience — sound, texture, temperature — changes when cutlery enters the picture.

Center vs. Side: The Strategist's Debate

If the fork-and-knife controversy was about cultural identity, the center-versus-side debate is about technique. Hyderabad-based comedian Saikiran brought it to the mainstream with a deadpan reel that played like a tactical briefing. His thesis: food vloggers have popularized the notion that the "right" way to eat masala dosa is from the center, where the potato filling sits. He calls this approach reckless.

Saikiran makes the case for side eating — tearing from the crispy edge, dunking in chutney or sambar, and working inward. His reasoning is grounded in temperature physics: the potato filling keeps the center hot, so the edges cool fastest and lose their crispness first. Eat from the outside in, and every bite is optimally crisp and warm. Dive into the middle, and you risk both burned fingers and soggy edges.

"If you begin in the middle and then reach the edges, it will lose its crispness," Saikiran explains. "Don't always be a warrior. Be a strategist."

A Larger Conversation About Indian Food and Western Norms

The dosa debate is part of a broader cultural reckoning with dining etiquette that flares up regularly on Indian social media. An "etiquette coach" demonstrating how to eat samosa with a fork and knife sparked a similar backlash last year, with critics asking why Western table manners should apply to foods designed for hand eating.

"Can we just stop teaching ourselves British table etiquettes and try eating Indian food the way it is supposed to be eaten?" one widely shared response read. "In which era are these guys living? Still validating themselves by acting like the West?"

For the diaspora, these debates carry extra resonance. Indian Americans navigating office lunches, restaurant dining, and cross-cultural meals regularly face subtle pressure to adopt cutlery-based norms — even for foods that lose something fundamental when you stop using your hands.

"Eating with your hands heightens the experience — it engages more than just taste, allowing texture, temperature, and aroma to play their part."

— Chef Stanley Coelho, Moxy Bengaluru Airport Prestige Tech Cloud

The Case for the Hand

Chef Stanley Coelho, speaking to Tasting Table about Indian dining customs, put it directly: "Eating with your hands heightens the experience." The technique — tearing small pieces, folding them neatly, using the right hand to scoop and deliver — is not a workaround for missing silverware. It is the intended interface between the food and the eater.

At the Hindu Temple Society of America in Queens, New York, Ganapathy Padmanabhan has demonstrated proper dosa technique for Zagat's "Stop Eating It Wrong" series, walking diners through how to crack the crispy exterior, pair each piece with the right accompaniment, and appreciate the dish as its makers intended.

The message, from Bengaluru to Queens, is consistent: the dosa is not incomplete without a fork. It is complete in your hands.
nri_angle: Indian Americans navigating cross-cultural dining face pressure to adopt cutlery norms for foods designed for hand eating; dosa technique debates resonate across the diaspora
author: Diaspora Desk
